layer2.mapping: A single play-call confrontation (offense call family vs defense call family under one condition complex) is a zero-sum two-person matrix game in expected points added: H(tau_1,tau_2) = EPA of the call pair, xi/eta = the mixed tendencies (probability vectors over call families). The minimax value v' is the play's game-theoretic value; the optimal mixed strategies are the unexploitable tendency mixes. The theorem guarantees a value exists for ANY EPA matrix, so the Coach-Mind sim can compute a conservative value for every down-distance matchup without assuming a pure-strategy equilibrium exists.
layer2.telemetry: Play-by-play EPA matrix by (offense family x defense family) per condition complex; empirical mixed-strategy frequencies vs the computed minimax mix; exploitability gap = regret of the observed tendency against a best-responding opponent model, held out across games.

Without numerical utility the zero-sum value concept of 17. collapses (66.2-66.3: 'we have at present no way to adscribe a zero-sum two-person game a value unless numerical utilities are available'). Ordinal-only preferences (indifference curves without probabilistic combination) do NOT yield numerical utility (A.3.4, third remark).

layer2.mapping: Every EPA-style model silently assumes the agent's preferences over risky football outcomes satisfy (3:A)-(3:C): a coach choosing between a safe field-goal attempt and a fourth-down gamble is combining utilities with probabilities, and the model's linear expectation is valid only if his utility is numerical up to affine gauge. The affine-uniqueness result is the license to calibrate utility from observed choice frequencies (revealed preference over lotteries) and the warning that any two calibrations must agree up to a positive linear map - otherwise one of them violates an axiom.
layer2.telemetry: Observed choice frequencies over repeated gamble-like decisions (fourth-down attempts, two-point conversions) stratified by score/clock; consistency tests of revealed preferences against transitivity and the Archimedean condition; affine-consistency check across separately calibrated utility scales.

For general non-zero-sum games the zero-sum axioms (25:3:b) must be replaced: the restricted characteristic function satisfies only (57:2:a), (57:2:c) plus v(S) + v(-S) <= v(I) (57.2.1), and the extended function of the fictitious-player game obeys the old axioms only on the enlarged player set.

layer2.mapping: Coalition values in the 22-player system: v(S) = the guaranteed expected-point value a subgroup S (e.g., the offensive line + QB protection unit, or a coverage shell) can secure against the complementary subgroup, computed as a minimax value over the subgroup's coordinated strategy space. Superadditivity is the audit that merging two units never destroys value: if charted data show v(S u T) < v(S) + v(T), the coordination model (or the transferable-utility assumption) is wrong - communication friction is a real breakdown regime the pure theory assumes away.
layer2.telemetry: Subgroup-level EPA differentials from charted assignments: value of the protection unit alone, of the coverage shell alone, and of the combined system; superadditivity residual v(S u T) - v(S) - v(T) per play family; negative residuals flag coordination failures to model explicitly.

primitives.verbatim_quote: We proceed to give the decisive definitions. In accordance with the suggestions of the preceding paragraphs we mean by a distribution or imputation a set of n numbers i, , a with 'the following properties (30:1) a, ^ v((0) for i = 1, - - , n, (30:2) a, = 0.

Both conditions compare/sum utility units; homogeneous. OCR note: the text layer renders alpha_i as 'a,', v((i)) as 'v((0)', and loses the summation sign of (30:2) (printed as 'i-l' below the line); the quote preserves that rendering.
primitives.assumptions: As printed: the game is a zero-sum n-person game with characteristic function v(S), taken in reduced form so that the total is zero; an imputation is 'a set of n numbers' satisfying (30:1) each player gets at least what he can guarantee alone, and (30:2) the numbers sum to zero. For general (non-zero-sum) games the conditions become (56:9) alpha_i >= v((i)) and (56:10) sum alpha_i <= v((1,...,n)) (56.8.2, PDF pp. 538-540): efficiency becomes an upper bound, not an equality.
primitives.breakdown_regime: In essential games no imputation is undominated by everything outside it ((31:M), referenced at PDF p. 288 footnote: an imputation never dominated from outside exists only in inessential games) - so individual rationality alone never pins down an outcome. If the transferable-utility assumption fails (utilities not numerically comparable across players), the sum conditions (30:2)/(56:10) are meaningless; Chapter XII (66.) discusses exactly this obstruction. The zero-sum equality sum = 0 also breaks for constant-sum games with nonzero total until the strategic-equivalence shift of 27.1 is applied.

layer2.mapping: An imputation is any feasible allocation of the play's total expected value among the 22 participants that respects each unit's security level: no player-group accepts less than it can guarantee alone (individual rationality), and the allocation exhausts the available value (efficiency). Roster-building and snap-count allocation are imputation problems: a playing-time distribution that gives a unit less than its standalone value is dominated and will be rejected by the coalition logic of the locker room; the sum constraint is the roster/snap budget.
layer2.telemetry: Per-unit standalone value estimates (EPA when the unit is on field vs replacement) and the observed allocation of snaps/targets/carries; flag allocations violating alpha_i >= v((i)); budget-exhaustion audit that assigned shares sum to the total available value.

The single-condition form (30:5:c): V is exactly the set of imputations undominated by any element of V.
primitives.assumptions: As printed: zero-sum n-person game in reduced form; domination is defined via an EFFECTIVE set S - 'the players who are convinced or can be convinced of the possibility of obtaining what they are offered' (30.1.2); all members of S must strictly prefer alpha to beta; the solution concept is a SET of imputations, not a single point, and corresponds to a 'standard of behavior' of everyday parlance (30.2.1, 4.6). The circularity of 'soundness' is explicitly acknowledged (30:A:a): an outside imputation dominating a member of V may still be rejected as 'unsound' because V is the accepted standard.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Domination is NOT transitive and can cycle: the relation is not an ordering, which is why solutions are generally non-unique (the essential zero-sum three-person game has a continuum of solutions, 32.2) and why Chapter XII must isolate acyclicity as the special condition restoring uniqueness (65:X). Effectiveness can fail for coalitions whose members cannot credibly commit (the fear of subsequent disadvantage, 29.2.2). For general non-zero-sum games the definition must be re-derived through the fictitious player: the literal extension (56:D) includes a condition interpreted as 'an influence which is definitely set to injure society as a whole' (56.10.3), and the authors restrict to (56:D:a) - domination via real-player coalitions only.

layer2.mapping: Locker-room and coordinator coalition dynamics as domination over allocations: a proposed game-plan allocation alpha dominates the incumbent beta if some effective coalition S (players who can jointly deviate - e.g., QB + receivers demanding target share, or a coordinator faction) can deliver its promised shares and every member strictly gains. A 'solution' is a stable standard of behavior - a set of allocations none of which is internally overturned and which collectively dominates every outsider. Multiple solutions = multiple stable team cultures; the sim must enumerate standards, not assume a unique equilibrium.
layer2.telemetry: Observed allocation changes (target shares, snap distributions, play-call mix) and the coalition that initiated them; stability audit: does any within-standard allocation get overturned by an effective coalition; count of distinct stable standards across seasons as evidence of solution multiplicity.

primitives.name: Strategic equivalence, unique reduced form (27:A), and the essential/inessential dichotomy (27.1-27.3, printed pp. 246-249; PDF pp. 269-272)
primitives.verbatim_quote: (27:A) We call a characteristic function v(S) reduced if and only if it satisfies (27:3). Then every characteristic function v(S) is in strategic equivalence with precisely one reduced v(S). This v(S) is given by the formulae (27:2) and (27:4), and we call it the reduced form of v(S).
primitives.latex: v'(S) = v(S) + \sum_{k\in S}\alpha_k^{0},\quad \sum_{k=1}^{n}\alpha_k^{0} = 0;\qquad \bar v((k)) = -\gamma\ \forall k,\quad \gamma = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n} v((k));\qquad \text{essential} \iff \gamma > 0,\quad \text{inessential} \iff \gamma = 0
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: v, v' = characteristic functions related by strategic equivalence (utility-unit set functions); alpha_k^0 = fixed constant added to player k's payoff (utility units), with sum_k alpha_k^0 = 0 so the zero-sum total is preserved (27:1)-(27:2); bar v = the unique reduced form with all one-player values equal (27:3); gamma = the common magnitude -bar v((k)) >= 0 (utility units); n = number of players (dimensionless). Inessential: reduced form identically zero, each player's value is his standalone amount 'even alone, irrespective of what the others are doing' (27.3.1, PDF p. 272). Essential: gamma > 0, a lone player loses gamma, coalitions have positive motive to form. All terms utility units; the shift is a change of each player's utility zero, gauge-invariant.
primitives.assumptions: As printed: strategic equivalence = adding constants alpha_k^0 to individual payoffs (a change of the origin of each player's utility scale, permitted because utility is unique only up to a linear transformation, p2); the sum-zero condition preserves the zero-sum character; every characteristic function is strategically equivalent to PRECISELY ONE reduced form (27:A). The quantity gamma is the invariant that classifies games: gamma = 0 inessential (no coalition can improve on standalone play), gamma > 0 essential.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Strategic equivalence preserves the strategic structure ONLY under the numerical-utility/transferable-utility assumptions; if utilities are merely ordinal the constant shifts are not licensed. The reduced-form normalization can obscure economically meaningful absolute levels (the authors note the change of unit to gamma = 1 'affects none of the strategically significant aspects' but is a convention). For general non-zero-sum games the analogous zero-reduced form (59:B) exists but the invariants change: |Gamma|_1 can be positive while |Gamma|_2 = 0 fails to follow (59.3.2, PDF p. 571), so zero-sum classification theorems do not transfer unchanged.

layer2.mapping: Before comparing any two games, schemes, or seasons, strip the gauge: additive constants per player (contract-year incentives, garbage-time stats, era scoring levels) are strategic-equivalence shifts, not strategic differences. The essential/inessential dichotomy is the audit of whether coordination matters at all: a unit whose members' standalone values already sum to the total (gamma = 0) gains nothing from scheme complexity - inessential games justify simple autonomous assignments; gamma > 0 is where coalition design (protection schemes, coverage rotations) creates value.
layer2.telemetry: Per-player standalone value vs unit-combined value across eras/teams; estimate gamma = combined value minus sum of standalone values; classify units essential/inessential before investing in coordination complexity; verify conclusions are invariant to additive per-player shifts.

primitives.name: Fictitious-player zero-sum extension of a general n-person game, eq. (56:2) (56.2.2, printed p. 506; PDF p. 529)
primitives.verbatim_quote: It consists of introducing a fictitious n + 1-st player who is assumed to lose the amount which the totality of the other n real players wins and vice versa. He must, of course, have no direct influence on the course of the game. Let us express this mathematically : Consider the general n-person game F of the players 1, , n, with the functions 3C*(ri, , rn) (k = 1, , n) in the sense of 11.2.3. We introduce the fictitious player n + 1 by defining n (56:2) 3Cn+1 (r,, , r w ) = - 3C*(n f , r). *i Thevariablesri, , rn are controlled by the real players 1, , n, respectively. They represent their influence on the course of the game. Since it is intended that the fictitious player have no influence on the course of the game, a variable r n+i which he controls, was not introduced. 2 In this way we obtain a zero-sum n + 1-person game, the zero-sum extension of F, to be denoted by T.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: H_k(tau_1,...,tau_n) = payoff function of real player k in the general n-person game Gamma (numerical-utility units); tau_k = strategy variable controlled by real player k (dimensionless index/choice); H_{n+1} = payoff of the fictitious (n+1)-st player, utility units, defined as the negative of the total real payoff; NO variable tau_{n+1} is introduced - the fictitious player has no influence on the course of the game; the extended game Tilde-Gamma is zero-sum: sum_{k=1}^{n+1} H_k = 0 identically (utility units cancel). OCR note: the text layer renders H as '3C' and the summation as 'n ... *i'; the quote preserves that rendering.
primitives.assumptions: As printed: the general n-person game has payoff functions H_k in the sense of 11.2.3; the fictitious player 'is assumed to lose the amount which the totality of the other n real players wins and vice versa' and 'must, of course, have no direct influence on the course of the game'; the real players' variables tau_1,...,tau_n are unchanged. The construction interprets an n-person general game as an (n+1)-person zero-sum game so the entire zero-sum theory can be reused (56.2.1).
primitives.breakdown_regime: The extension is NOT a free lunch: the fictitious player, though a dummy in moves, is NOT a dummy in coalitions - 'no player or group of players will pay a (positive) compensation for his cooperation' yet his presence changes which imputations are dominated (56.4, PDF p. 531). The solutions of the general game form only a SUBSET of the solutions of its zero-sum extension ((56:I:a), 56.12); the literal domination definition produces the pathological condition (56:D:b) interpreted as injuring society as a whole, forcing the restriction to real-player coalitions (56.10.3). The whole two-stage procedure (solve two-person games -> characteristic function -> n-person solution) is flagged in 66.4 as a weakness: 'the necessity to proceed in two stages'.

layer2.mapping: Football is not zero-sum at the league level (both teams can gain entertainment value, injury costs are shared losses), so the 22-player system is a general game. The fictitious-player construction is the formal license to reuse zero-sum solvers: append a dummy 'house' player whose payoff is minus the total EPA, solve the extended zero-sum game, then restrict to solutions where the dummy is never bought into a coalition. The breakdown regime is the modeling warning: any sim result that depends on the dummy player joining a coalition (e.g., treating the league's shared interest as an active strategic agent) is an artifact of the extension, not a property of the real game.
layer2.telemetry: Audit of simulated coalition structures: flag any solution imputation where the dummy player's component is used to enforce domination; verify restricted-solution membership (56:I) by re-checking domination with real-player coalitions only; compare general-game outputs against direct non-zero-sum simulation.

(65:K) = every nonempty subset of D possesses maxima; for finite D this is equivalent to acyclicity and to strict acyclicity (65:O:c). The construction peels off maxima B_i and their dominated followers C_i until D is exhausted; (65:V) any solution equals V_0, (65:W) V_0 is a solution, hence (65:X) uniqueness.
primitives.breakdown_regime: For INFINITE D the equivalence breaks: acyclicity is necessary but strict acyclicity only sufficient for unique solutions in every subset (65:Y, 65:Z, PDF pp. 624-625); the gap - acyclic but not strictly acyclic infinite sets satisfying (B*) - 'can only be bridged by a study of' such sets and is left open (65.8.3). Domination in actual games is generally NOT acyclic (the three-person game cycles), which is precisely why vNM solutions are multiple; the theorem marks the exact boundary where the multiplicity collapses. The authors connect the failure of acyclicity to monopolistic market situations (65.9, PDF p. 626).

layer2.mapping: When is a team's decision culture uniquely determined? Model the set D of candidate standards (play-call philosophies, allocation norms) with the domination relation 'a coalition can overturn beta for alpha'. If D is finite and domination is acyclic (no rock-paper-scissors loop of standards), the peeling construction gives ONE stable standard - the maximal elements and everything they dominate. Cyclic domination (scheme A beats scheme B beats scheme C beats scheme A, the coordinator carousel) is the mathematical signature of multiple coexisting standards and persistent instability; the theorem tells the sim when to expect a unique culture and when multiplicity is structural, not noise.
layer2.telemetry: Directed graph of observed standard-overturn events (coordinator changes, scheme replacements) with edge = 'coalition overturned'; cycle detection on the graph; finite-horizon check that the peeling process terminates; acyclicity violations predict recurring coordinator turnover rather than convergence.

reasoning_traces.think: Von Neumann and Morgenstern's 1944 monograph, read here in the third edition of 1953, is the moment strategic interaction became a mathematical discipline, and for a football decision foundry it is simultaneously the deepest license and the sharpest set of warnings in the entire corpus. The architecture is a ladder of reductions, and each rung has an exact validity condition. At the bottom sits the zero-sum two-person game. The Main Theorem of 17.6 states that for every bilinear payoff form K(xi,eta) on the strategy simplexes, Max Min K equals Min Max K: a saddle point exists, the game has a value, and it makes no difference who finds out whose strategy. The coefficients are 'absolutely unrestricted' - a perfectly arbitrary matrix. This is the theorem that lets the Coach-Mind simulator assign a conservative value to any play-call confrontation without first proving an equilibrium exists. But the theorem is about MIXED strategies. Matching Pennies and Stone, Paper, Scissors are the book's own examples where no pure-strategy saddle point exists: special strict determinateness fails while general strict determinateness holds. Translated to football, a play-call matchup with no pure best response - the run-pass option dilemma, the blitz-pickup guessing game - still has a value, but only in tendencies, only in mixes. Any analysis that reports 'the best call' against a thinking opponent in such a matchup is reporting an object the theorem says does not exist. The value lives in the probability vector over calls, and the exploitability of a predictable tendency is exactly the gap A' = v'_2 - v'_1 that the theorem proves is zero at optimal mixes and positive away from them. The second rung is utility, and it is where most sports analytics silently overreaches. The entire minimax machinery presupposes NUMERICAL utility, and Chapter I section 3 plus the Appendix earn that presupposition axiomatically: a complete ordering of utilities, the Archimedean combining conditions (3:B:c) and (3:B:d), and the compound-lottery algebra (3:C:b) together imply that utility is a number up to a linear transformation - unique up to positive slope and zero shift. The authors are candid that these are idealizations: Appendix A.3 explicitly anticipates that completeness or the compound-lottery axiom may fail for real individuals, and Chapter XII section 66 states plainly that without numerical utilities 'we have at present no way to adscribe a zero-sum two-person game a value'. Every expected-points model in the foundry is therefore making a behavioral claim: that the coach's preferences over risky outcomes satisfy (3:A)-(3:C). When a coach repeatedly makes choices that violate transitivity or the Archimedean condition - refusing a gamble at one probability but accepting a compound version of it - the utility representation is not merely noisy, it is undefined, and the minimax value computed from his stated preferences is an artifact. The affine-uniqueness result is also a calibration protocol: two independently revealed-preference utility scales for the same decision-maker must agree up to a positive linear map, and a failure of that test is evidence that one of the axiom sets was violated in elicitation. The third rung is the passage from two persons to n. The characteristic function v(S) assigns to every coalition the value it can guarantee against its complement, and its three axioms - v(empty) = 0, v(-S) = -v(S), and superadditivity for disjoint coalitions - are proved conceptually: S can get v(S) and no more, T can get v(T) and no more, so S union T can get at least v(S) + v(T) even if the subcoalitions fail to cooperate with each other. The proof is a masterpiece of minimal assumptions, and its football content is precise: merging two units never destroys value IF the units can operate independently within the merged coalition. Communication friction, assignment conflicts, and tempo mismatches are exactly the physical mechanisms that can make the superadditivity residual negative in charted data, and when that happens the transferable-utility coalition model is falsified for that play family. The imputation definitions (30:1)-(30:2) then say what a feasible allocation is: everyone gets at least their standalone security value, and the shares sum to the total. Domination (30:4) says when an effective coalition can overturn one allocation for another, and a solution (30:5) is a set of allocations that is internally stable and externally dominant - a 'standard of behavior'. The crucial structural fact, which the foundry must internalize, is that solutions are SETS and are generally NOT unique: the essential three-person game already has a continuum of them. A team culture, a coordinator's play-call philosophy, a locker-room allocation norm - these are vNM solutions, and multiplicity is structural, not estimation noise.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The hidden state of modern game-theoretic sports modeling was created by two earlier scars. The first is the minimax lineage the book itself documents in the footnote to 17.6: von Neumann's 1928 'Zur Theorie der Gesellschaftsspiele' proved the theorem with topology and functional calculus; his 1937 economic-equilibrium paper connected it to Brouwer's fixed-point theorem; Kakutani simplified it in 1941; Ville gave the first elementary proof in 1938; and the 1944 book elementarizes it further through the convexity theory of Chapter 16. Every 'equilibrium exists' claim in a sports simulator descends from that chain of proofs, and the book's own remark that two widely different economic problems lead to the same 'Min-Max type' problem is the origin of treating market competition and strategic sport as one mathematical species. The second scar is the utility lineage: Bernoulli's St. Petersburg resolution, the Austrian School's ordinalism, and the indifference-curve tradition that refused numerical utility. The axioms (3:A)-(3:C) are the 1944 settlement of that dispute, and the Appendix's candid admission that the axioms may need modification is the wound that later behavioral economics reopened.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Under pressure the three minds are playing different games. The coach's comfort call is a pure-strategy instinct in a game the theorem says has only mixed solutions: he wants a single 'best call' because his utility over risky outcomes violates the compound-lottery axiom under stress, collapsing the numerical representation the minimax value requires. The defensive coordinator models the coach's tendency as a fixed vector and best-responds to it - he is computing Min Max against a known xi, exactly the 'found out' scenario of 14.7, and his trap works because the coach's mix is degenerate. The quarterback's internal clock truncates the observation window, so his posterior over the defense's mix is computed on a censored sample; recursively, the DC knows the QB's clock and designs the look that maximizes the divergence between the QB's censored posterior and the true mix. Each agent models the others' utility representation and information partition; the belief clash is sharpest on third-and-long, where the coach's pure-strategy comfort, the DC's best-response to a degenerate mix, and the QB's censored posterior each assign a different value to the same play.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Three vetoes compose from the first three rungs. The pure-strategy veto: in any matchup without a pure saddle point - the book's Matching Pennies class - a call recommendation that names a single best action is vetoed, because the theorem locates the value only in the mix; the high-EV 'just run it' comfort call is rejected when the exploitability gap of that degenerate tendency is positive. The utility veto: when revealed-preference tests show the decision-maker violates (3:A)-(3:C) under pressure, any expected-utility computation over his choices is vetoed as undefined, not merely uncertain; the sim must fall back to ordinal dominance or refuse the comparison. The superadditivity veto: a coalition-based value estimate whose charted residual v(S u T) - v(S) - v(T) is negative is vetoed for that play family, because the transferable-utility assumption the characteristic function requires has been falsified by the physics of communication and assignment.

reasoning_traces.think: The upper rungs of the monograph - strategic equivalence, the fictitious player, and the acyclicity boundary - are where the foundry's modeling hygiene is decided. Strategic equivalence (27:A) says every characteristic function is equivalent to precisely one reduced form, obtained by adding constants to individual payoffs with sum zero. This is a gauge theory of value: because utility is unique only up to a linear transformation, shifting each player's zero is strategically invisible. The football content is immediate. Era scoring levels, contract-year incentives, garbage-time accumulation - these are additive constants per player, and any comparison of schemes or seasons that is not invariant to them is comparing gauges, not strategies. The essential/inessential dichotomy is the invariant that survives: gamma = 0 means no coalition can improve on standalone play, and scheme complexity is wasted; gamma > 0 means coordination creates value and coalition design is the whole game. The foundry should compute gamma for every unit before investing in coordination complexity, and should treat a gamma = 0 unit's elaborate scheme as a category error. The fictitious-player extension (56:2) is the book's most subtle engineering move and its most instructive failure mode. Football is not zero-sum: both teams can gain, injuries are shared losses, the league's interest is not any team's negative. To reuse the zero-sum theory, the authors append a dummy player whose payoff is minus the total real payoff, with no strategy variable - he cannot influence the course of the game. The construction is formally flawless, but the book is scrupulous about what it does NOT license. The dummy is a dummy in moves but not in coalitions: his presence changes which imputations are dominated, the solutions of the general game form only a subset of the solutions of the extension, and the literal extension of domination produces a condition the authors interpret as 'an influence which is definitely set to injure society as a whole' - which they explicitly restrict away. The foundry's sim must carry the same restriction: any result that depends on the dummy joining a coalition, any 'league interest' treated as an active strategic agent, is an artifact of the extension. The authors' own summary in 66.4 - that the weakness of the theory 'lies in the necessity to proceed in two stages', solving two-person games to build the characteristic function before solving the n-person game - is the honest statement of a limitation every modern multi-agent simulator inherits. Finally, Chapter XII's acyclicity theorem (65:X) draws the exact boundary of uniqueness. For a finite set of alternatives D with an acyclic domination relation, the peeling construction - take the maxima B_i, remove them and everything they dominate C_i, repeat - terminates and yields the one and only solution. For infinite D the equivalence of acyclicity and strict acyclicity breaks, and the book leaves the gap open. The football reading is a theory of organizational stability: when the domination graph over candidate standards is acyclic, a unique stable culture exists and the peeling process finds it; when it cycles - scheme A overturns scheme B overturns scheme C overturns scheme A, the coordinator carousel - multiplicity is structural and persistent turnover is the prediction, not a failure of estimation. The book even connects the failure of acyclicity to monopolistic market situations, which is the mathematical signature of power asymmetries that prevent convergence. Taken together, the eight primitives form a complete audit stack: value existence (minimax), utility representation (axioms), coalition value (characteristic function), feasible allocation (imputation), stability (domination/solution), gauge invariance (strategic equivalence), non-zero-sum licensing (fictitious player), and uniqueness boundary (acyclicity). Each is a theorem with printed assumptions and a printed breakdown regime. The monograph's deepest lesson for the foundry is that every one of these objects is conditional: the value exists only in mixes, the utility only under axioms, the coalition value only under transferable utility, the unique solution only under acyclicity. A simulator that reports any of them unconditionally is reporting fiction.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The strategic-equivalence apparatus descends from the utility settlement of Chapter I: because utility is numerical only up to a linear transformation, the additive shifts of 27.1 are the residual gauge freedom, and the reduced form is the gauge fixing. The fictitious-player construction is the 1944 answer to a scar the authors name explicitly in 56.1: dropping the zero-sum restriction makes 'characteristic functions, domination, solutions ... no longer defined', a conceptual crisis rather than a technical one, and the n+1 embedding is the resolution that preserves the entire existing theory at the cost of a dummy. The acyclicity chapter descends from the observation, forced by the three-person game's continuum of solutions, that domination is not an ordering; the partial-ordering and acyclicity taxonomy of 65.2-65.6 is the systematic attempt to find where uniqueness survives, and the open gap for infinite sets (65.8.3) is the wound later fixed-point and kernel theories of stable sets would address. The market applications of Chapter XI - Boehm-Bawerk's marginal pairs recovered as a theorem in 61.5 - are the book's own proof that the apparatus reproduces classical economics, and the monopoly-acyclicity connection of 65.9 is the seed of later industrial-organization game theory.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: The general manager, the coordinator, and the quarterback hold different beliefs about which rung of the ladder they are on. The GM thinks in imputations: roster allocation is a distribution problem, and he assumes a unique stable allocation exists - an implicit acyclicity assumption about the locker room's domination graph. The coordinator knows the graph cycles: he has lived the carousel where his scheme overturns his predecessor's and is overturned by his successor's, and he models the GM as believing in a uniqueness the dynamics do not support. The QB models both: he knows the GM's allocation norm is one vNM solution among many, and he knows the coordinator's current standard is unstable, so he hedges his own effort allocation across standards rather than committing to one. Recursively, the coordinator models the QB's hedging and designs plays that work under multiple standards, while the GM reads the hedging as disloyalty to the 'sound' allocation - exactly the (30:A:a) circularity where an outside imputation is rejected as unsound because the accepted standard defines soundness. The belief clash is a three-level theory-of-mind stack over solution multiplicity.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Three vetoes from the upper rungs. The gauge veto: any cross-era or cross-team comparison whose conclusion changes under additive per-player shifts is vetoed as a gauge artifact; only strategic-equivalence invariants like gamma may drive decisions. The dummy veto: any sim output whose coalition structure or domination enforcement uses the fictitious player - any 'league interest' or 'shared welfare' agent acting strategically - is vetoed as an extension artifact, and the result must be re-derived with real-player coalitions only per the (56:D:a) restriction. The acyclicity veto: a prediction of unique organizational convergence is vetoed when the observed domination graph over standards contains a cycle; the theorem says multiplicity is structural there, and the high-confidence 'this culture will stabilize' call is rejected in favor of the turnover prediction. Physics of communication, psychology of soundness, and the mathematics of domination agree: the unconditional claim is the fiction.

universal_lens: Von Neumann and Morgenstern supply a polymath audit ladder for any strategic claim: name the game form (zero-sum two-person, zero-sum n-person, general), verify the utility representation axioms before computing expectations, declare the coalition value function and its superadditivity, state the allocation's individual-rationality and efficiency constraints, identify the domination relation and whether it is acyclic, and strip gauge before comparing. A strategic number without these declarations is a metaphor, not a value; the ladder applies identically to markets, coalitions, and football.
gsi_mapping: The utility axioms (3:A)-(3:C) formalize when a patient's or athlete's preferences over risky health outcomes admit a numerical representation, licensing expected-utility treatment decisions; the affine-uniqueness result is the calibration protocol for revealed-preference health utility scales. The characteristic-function superadditivity audit applies to multi-modal rehabilitation coalitions (strength + mobility + load management): a negative residual falsifies the independent-operation assumption. The acyclicity boundary predicts when a clinical decision protocol converges to a unique standard versus cycling among competing guidelines.
gse_mapping: Coach-Mind computes minimax values over EPA matrices for every down-distance matchup, reports optimal mixed tendencies rather than pure best calls, and audits exploitability of observed mixes; the utility-axiom test gates every expected-value computation over coach choices; strategic-equivalence invariants (gamma) classify units before scheme investment; the fictitious-player restriction forbids treating shared league interest as a strategic agent; acyclicity detection on the coordinator-standards graph predicts turnover. Internal only: no sportsbook odds as inputs, no publication from this lane.
